transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Chris Lane (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Tom Miller (Meridian CTO), Aisha Rahman (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Gomez (VP Product)

Summary (auto): quick optimize walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations; walked through a cost model with example hit rates and token assumptions; agreed to run an initial benchmark; security and VPC questions flagged.

00:00 Chris: ok everyone, thanks for joining on a Sunday \u001F appreciate it, um Tom, Aisha, Sofia \u001F you there?
00:07 Tom: yeah hi, thanks, sorry for the late change.
00:10 Priya: no worries. we'll run through the Optimize recommendations \u001F batching, prefix vs KV cache \u001F and then show a simple cost model with hit-rate sensitivity. excuse any auto-transcript weirdness.
00:25 Aisha: great, high level we get ~120k requests/day today, avg 350 tokens/request, tail up to 1k tokens for a subset. latency target is sub-300ms for interactive flows.
00:40 Chris: ok that's helpful. and are you running any in-house quantized models or are y'all strictly hitting hosted APIs now?
00:48 Aisha: currently using a mix \u001F some internal endpoints (FP16) for internal tools and OpenAI for customer-facing features; costs are getting rough.
00:56 Priya: sounds typical. so Optimize suggestions: 1) continuous batching at the request router to increase throughput without blowing latency SLOs, 2) prefix caching for short deterministic prompts, and 3) a KV cache layer for session-based KV cache (we call it KV cache) for long-context reuse. we'll show numbers.
01:20 Sofia: can you just clarify prefix vs KV? i've heard both but confused about tradeoffs.
01:26 Priya: yeah prefix cache is basically caching the model's output embeddings/tokens for repeated fixed prompts, think: greeting prompt, static instructions. it's cheap but hit rates depend on exact prompt matching. KV cache stores intermediate KV tensors for transformer layers so during generation you can reuse previous context, huge wins for multi-turn chat. it's more infra heavy but bigger per-token savings. transcript note: K V sometimes transcribed as \"kay-vee\" or \"kv cahche\".
02:05 Chris: and in some cases you do both \u001F prefix for identical prompts + KV to reduce compute on long sessions.
02:12 Tom: ok, show us the cost numbers.
02:15 Priya: right \u001F here's a simple model we walked through in the deck: assume baseline hosted gpt-like model at $0.0004 per input token and $0.0016 per output token (example numbers, not final pricing). under current workload: 120k req/day * 350 avg tokens -> ~42M tokens/day. at baseline that's X dollars, roughly $16k/month.
02:42 Aisha: wait that seems low relative to our bill \u001F are you including embedding/other pipelines?
02:46 Priya: good call \u001F we kept to inference only for this slide; your pipeline also does contextual retrieval and reranking which adds. for the demo we focused on text gen costs.
02:58 Priya: now with batching: if we enable continuous batching tuned to your latency SLO, we can increase GPU utilization and reduce per-token cost. example: batching reduces effective per-token cost by ~18-25% depending on batch size and sequence length distribution.
03:16 Chris: and KV cache: if you get a 40% KV hit rate across multi-turn sessions, you can reduce compute for those requests by up to 50-60% because you avoid recomputing earlier layers. combined with batching we'd usually show 40-55% total cost reduction in our model.
03:35 Sofia: 40% hit rate realistic?
03:37 Aisha: for support chat maybe \u001F but product interactions less. we estimate 20-30% overall.
03:42 Priya: yep that's why we present sensitivity: for 20% KV hit-rate + 20% batching improvement -> end-to-end ~30% cost drop. the spreadsheet has sliders.
04:00 Tom: how does dedicated vs hosted factor in? if we go dedicated reserved capacity, is it cheaper?
04:06 Chris: dedicated gives predictable throughput and often lower unit costs if you're committing. but then you trade off utilization risk. our Optimize tool suggests hybrid routing: host burst + dedicated for steady state.
04:18 Aisha: security is a huge thing for us \u001F PCI scope is a concern, any VPC/on-prem options?
04:23 Dana: yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem options. for Meridian we can propose customer-managed VPC peering and KMS/HSM integration. we'll share SOC2 and network diagrams after this call.
04:35 Tom: great. SSO and audit logs?
04:38 Dana: SSO via SAML/Okta supported; RBAC and per-route audit logs available in the Console.
04:45 Priya: back to perf: we also showed how quantization affects batching \u001F 4-bit quant models change kernel selection and often increase batching efficiency (smaller memory footprint) but sometimes slightly up model latency. tradeoff table in slide 6.
05:05 Aisha: i wish the transcript showed the table. (laughter)
05:10 Priya: i will send the deck and the spreadsheet. note: some auto-typos in the transcript \u001F \"quantize\" sometimes becomes \"congeal\".
05:22 Chris: let's walk a quick worked example: assume 42M tokens/day baseline, 30% batching improvement gives effective cost -> 0.7 * baseline token compute cost. KV with 25% hit rate reduces compute on those tokens by 50%, so aggregate compute becomes 0.875 * baseline (example math inline). overall cost drop ~30-45% depending on numbers.
06:05 Tom: can Redwood run a benchmark with our real traffic? we'd have to scrub PCI-sensitive fields but we can synthetic-ize tokens.
06:12 Priya: yes we typically run a 1-2 week benchmark window. what we need: sample traffic distribution (seq length CDF), 1k representative sessions, and an infra contact to provision a test VPC. we provide the harness and collection script.
06:30 Chris: action: Priya will send test harness and recommended config; Tom to provision peering.
06:36 Tom: ok.
06:40 Sofia: any gotchas on KV warmup? if sessions are cold, hit-rate low.
06:44 Priya: good point \u001F warmup matters. KV is best for repeated sessions or when you can persist per-user session state. We propose TTL policies and eviction strategies to keep memory in check. e.g., 24-48 hour TTL for active users.
07:02 Aisha: what's the infra cost for KV (RAM/GPU memory)?
07:06 Priya: KV stores are primarily in-GPU cache for fastest path; memory overhead depends on model size and cache entries. rough rule: KV entries ~ model_hidden_size * seq_len * 2 (bytes) per token. in practice we modeled the mem cost into the spreadsheet as additional reserved-GPU capacity.
07:28 Chris: also note, for some customers a hybrid approach (prefix cache in Redis + small KV cache in GPU) balances cost. prefix hits served from Redis are extremely cheap per-hit.
07:40 Tom: are there any compliance implications storing KV?
07:43 Dana: KV entries are transient. we can disable persistence, encrypt in transit and at rest, and provide audit logs. for PCI workloads we'd recommend dedicated Private deployment and narrow the session retention window.
08:00 Priya: moving on, here's the quick demo of Console Optimize tab \u001F (screen share sounds) \u001F shows per-route token breakdown, suggested batching window, and projected monthly cost savings given hit rates. note: screenshot references in transcript are \"slide 8\" and \"console view\".
08:22 Priya: demo noise: the console will show a slider for KV hit-rate and batching improvement; updating sliders re-computes cost instantly.
08:30 Sofia: useful. can we upload our internal seq length histogram?
08:33 Priya: yes there's an import CSV \u001F that will auto-fit the model and give recommended batching/quant profiles.
08:40 Aisha: on the quant profiles, how intrusive is model swapping? do we need to re-run evals?
08:44 Priya: we recommend a canary rollout: 5% of traffic on quantized variant, measure quality via eval set. Redwood Optimize can run quality regression tests and alert if drift > threshold.
09:00 Tom: ok. question: if we choose dedicated, how quickly can we get a pilot?
09:04 Chris: typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for reserved pool + infra setup; benchmark can run in parallel if you provide peering quickly.
09:12 Aisha: budget \u001F what's the delta vs current spend?
09:15 Priya: depends on commitment, but with a 30-40% expected improvement from batching+KV we project 6-12 month payback if you commit to dedicated capacity; the spreadsheet has NPV scenarios.
09:30 Chris: just to call out: these are modeled numbers; the benchmark will confirm.
09:35 Tom: who are we coordinating with on your side for the test infra?
09:38 Chris: Priya will be the SE lead; Dana will handle security docs; I'm the commercial contact.
09:44 Priya: ok small demo note: some automatic captions mislabelled \"KV\" as \"k v\" and \"prefix\" as \"pre-fix\" \u001F ignore.
09:52 Aisha: thank you.
10:00 -- transcript proceeds with more Q&A until 45 minutes --
10:12 Priya: one more technical detail: batching window \u001F there's a tradeoff curve: bigger window increases batch size and throughput but adds queueing latency. we recommend latency SLO-driven windows, example: for 300ms SLO keep max window 40ms for interactive flows, 100ms acceptable for async.
10:40 Tom: good. how do we measure end-to-end impact on p99?
10:44 Priya: Redwood Console exposes p50/p90/p99 per-route; we also instrument kernel queue times and show expected p99 shifts in the cost model.
11:05 Chris: let's capture next steps now: I'll send the cost-model spreadsheet, Priya sends harness and we'll schedule benchmark for next week, Dana shares SOC2 + VPC/KMS docs.
11:23 Tom: solid. any other blockers?
11:27 Sofia: legal on PCI side may want contract language around data handling \u001F we'll loop in procurement.
11:33 Dana: we can provide standard PCI addendum and compliance slide.
11:36 Chris: ok great. thanks all.
11:40 Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: medium \u001F occasional word swaps (quantize -> congeal), acronym parsing errors (KV -> \"kay vee\"), and missing punctuation.
